files.text:
chart

Counted out in silver

The denarius was Rome's silver coin for four and a half centuries, first struck around 211 BC and marked X for the ten bronze asses it was worth. Its half, the quinarius, was marked V. Each was struck by hand, one blank at a time, between two engraved dies, so no two came out alike.

Here every value is counted out in fives on a wool tunic woven in Roman Egypt, the way a money-changer laid coins on a cloth. Each coin stands for the same amount, which the key gives: two years, three or four, whatever lets the longest row fill the cloth. A real quinarius stands for half of it. Hover a coin to count up to it. Tap one to turn it over.

on a page

The waters of Rome

In AD 97 Sextus Julius Frontinus was made curator of Rome's water supply. He had the aqueducts surveyed, found where their water was being stolen, and wrote it all down.

His lengths are in paces, a thousand to the Roman mile.

# denarii A bar chart counted out in Roman silver on a real cloth. You write a plain `` of your own numbers, and each row is laid out as a line of real denarii, one coin to a unit, in fives, each coin resting a little on the one before, with a real quinarius (the half-denarius) for a half unit. The count lies on the plain field of a real wool tunic fragment from Egypt (400s-600s), between its own two tapestry bands, with its corner band in the gutter beside the names. Every coin is a separate museum photograph of a separate hand-struck coin, cut from its ground and shown at its true size relative to the others. Hover or tap a coin and it lifts off the cloth and reads the count up to it. Tap it to turn it over: what you see is that coin's own reverse. With more than one column of numbers there is a switch, and the coins are counted on or gathered off as the values change. Without JS it is the table. With JS the table is still the content: its cells stay in place for assistive tech, and the coins are drawn in one extra, `aria-hidden` cell per row. ```html
Nine emperors Years on the throne, and age at death.
EmperorYears reignedAge at death
Augustus40.675
Tiberius22.577
``` ```js import { denarii, count } from './denarii.js'; const chart = denarii(figure, { minCoins: 15, maxCoins: 40 }); chart.show(1); // the second column of numbers chart.select(0); // read a row (dims the others, says it in the live region) chart.turn(0, 3); // turn row 0's fourth coin over chart.recount(); // count every row out again (e.g. after you change the table's numbers and call it afresh) chart.column; chart.unit; figure.addEventListener('denarii:change', (e) => e.detail); // {column, name} figure.addEventListener('denarii:select', (e) => e.detail); // {row, label, value, column} chart(); // destroy: removes the coins, the switch, the key and listeners; leaves the plain table count(23, 5); // {n: 4, half: true, slots: 5}, the coins a value takes ``` Each row's first cell is its label (a ``), and every other cell is a number. A cell's number is read from its text (`1,240`, `£3.2`, `−4` all work), or from `data-value` when the text says something else (`3.2m`). The text, exactly as you wrote it, is what is shown at the end of the row. ## In life, and here | In life | Here | |---|---| | The denarius was Rome's silver coin from about 211 BC until the middle of the third century AD. It was worth ten bronze asses and was marked X for it. Its half, the quinarius, was marked V. | One denarius is one unit of your data, and one quinarius is half a unit. The key under the chart says what a unit is (`2 yrs`, `1 yr`). The coin size is set by the width (about one coin per 30 px, at least 15 to a full row). Then, for each column on its own, the unit is the smallest of 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6 or 8 × 10ⁿ for which that column's longest value still fits. Each column's coins are then sized so its longest row reaches about 90% of the cloth's field (85% on a phone), with its number still after it. Switching columns can change the unit (the key says so) and the coins' size; coins that stay slide and resize to their new places, and the rows keep their spacing. | | Each coin was struck by hand. Blanks were made so many to the pound of silver, not each to an exact size. A blank was set on the lower die and hit once with the upper die held in the hand. So coins of the same issue differ in size, centring, flan shape and wear, and no two are alike. | Every coin is its own photograph: 144 denarii and 3 quinarii from the Art Institute of Chicago, struck between 200 BC and the 240s AD (and one, of Galerius, about 307), obverse and reverse. Each is shown at the diameter the museum recorded (14 to 22 mm) on one scale. All coins sit on the same pitch, so length stays honest, each centred in a slot as wide as the widest denarius, and each coin rests a little on the one before. No coin appears twice in a row, and adjacent rows draw from different parts of the pool. Faces are upright, as the museum photographed them. The purple-black toners are culled from the pool by measured lightness and colour cast. | | Coins were counted out on a table, often onto a cloth, one by one, set down beside the last, and money was reckoned in ones and fives (I, V, X). In Roman Egypt, tunics were woven in one piece on the loom: a plain wool or linen ground, with tapestry bands and ornaments worked into it as it grew. | Coins are laid in fives, with a small gap between each five. The cloth is a real tunic fragment, shown untouched. It is cut from the museum's mount along its own torn edge, its two losses open to the page, and it is never stretched: one scale, chosen so that its plain field between the bands holds the rows. Measured in the demo, that is 1.4 to 1.6 times the coins' scale on a desktop and 1.8 to 2.3 times on a phone, and it is cropped only where the chart ends. No lines are drawn on it, so the fives and the value at each row's end do the reading. When the chart scrolls into view each row is counted out: one coin after another, each set down just short of its place and sliding the rest of the way on the cloth. Constant friction gives an even deceleration, so it eases out quadratically. When the numbers change, coins that stay slide to their new places, new coins are counted on from the end of the row, and coins no longer needed are gathered back. | | Each coin had two faces, struck by two dies: usually a head and a type, often the moneyer's name. | Tap a coin (or press Enter on a row) and it turns over to its own reverse, photographed with it. | There is no transformation and no payoff at the end: the coins are the bars, from the first frame to the last. What it does not do: negative values (they count as nothing), stacked or grouped bars, and fractions finer than a half unit. A value is rounded to the nearest half coin, a quarter or more becoming a quinarius, and the exact value is always written at the end of the row. ## Options | Option | Attribute | Default | | |---|---|---|---| | `unit` | `data-unit` | chosen | What one denarius stands for. | | `max` | `data-max` | the largest value | The scale's end, to compare several charts. | | `minCoins` | `data-min-coins` | `15` | The fewest coins a full-width row is sized for. | | `maxCoins` | `data-max-coins` | `40` | The most coins in any row. | | `cloth` | `data-cloth` | `true` | `false` lays the count on the page instead of the cloth. | | `coin` | `data-coin` | `--dn-coin` | The largest slot, in px. | | `column` | `data-column` | `0` | Which number column to show first. | | `face` | `data-face` | `obv` | `obv`, `rev`, or `mixed` (as if the coins had been thrown down). | | `seed` | `data-seed` | random | The draw of coins. Each load draws differently unless this is set. | | `unitLabel` | `data-unit-label` | | A short unit for the key and readings (`mi`, `t`), or singular and plural as `yr|yrs`. | | `label` | `data-label` | `Show` | The switch's group label. | | `src` | `data-src` | `assets/coins.json` beside the script | The pool. `coins/` sits beside it. | ## Theming Uses `--paper`, `--ink` (names and numbers on the cloth), `--ink-2`, `--ink-3`, `--rule`, `--accent` (focus), `--serif`, `--sans`. | Variable | Default | | |---|---|---| | `--dn-coin` | `60px` | The largest slot. | | `--dn-min` | `20px` | The smallest slot. | | `--dn-reserve` | `64px` | Room after the longest row for its number. | | `--dn-label` | `26%` | The most the label column takes. | Below 640 px of its own width (so it works in a sidebar too) each name goes above its row on the cloth, the corner band moves off to the left, and the coins take the full width. When the cloth is shown large (a phone, many rows), the full-resolution crop of its left side (`cloth-near.webp`, 9.9 px/mm) is used, so the weave stays sharp. ## Accessibility The table stays a real table: caption, column headers and every number are in the accessibility tree. When there is a switch, the caption is shown once, visually, above it (an `aria-hidden` copy) and kept on the table for screen readers. Inactive columns are visually hidden but still read. The coins, the cloth, the key and the readings are `aria-hidden`. The table is one tab stop. Up and Down read the rows, Home and End go to the first and last, Left and Right change the column, and Enter turns the row's coins over. A polite live region (role `status`) says the row and its value, or the new column. The switch is real buttons with `aria-pressed`, 44 px tall. In forced colours the coins are hidden and the table is shown as a table. **Reduced motion:** the coins are simply there, with no counting, sliding or lifting. Turning a coin over swaps its face at once. ## Cost The cloth: `cloth.webp` 1.5 MB (the whole fragment at 6.5 px/mm), or `cloth-near.webp` 1.7 MB on screens that show it large. Only one is loaded. The pool: 294 webp files, 3.5 MB on disk, about 12 KB each. A chart loads only the coins it shows (the demo's first chart 83 obverses on a desktop, about 1 MB), and a reverse only when its coin is turned. The JSON is 18 KB. No canvas and no rAF loop: coins are `` elements with WAAPI animations that end. Idle, nothing runs. A ResizeObserver relays the rows out when the chart's width changes. ## How it was made `tools/engine/jobs/sf-chart-work/`: `cut.py` finds each face on the museum's flat grey ground (exactly RGB 113, σ 0.2, so a distance threshold, opening, closing and hole fill find the coin with its own rim, nicks and flan cracks), gives it a 1.6 px soft edge pulled in by 0.8 px, and keeps the two largest regions as obverse and reverse. `export.py` scales every face to 8 px per millimetre of its recorded diameter and writes `assets/coins.json` and `assets/credits.json`. `tone.py` measures each obverse's lightness and cast for the cull. `cloth.py` cuts the tunic fragment from its mount by chroma (the mount is pale, low-chroma linen), keeps losses over 3 mm open, crops just outside the two bands and records the field's edges in `assets/cloth.json`. Masters (3000 px coins, the 6345 px TIFF) and both cloth files passed `engine.py inspect`. The hunt, the contact sheets and the reasons are in `assets/PICK.md`. ## Credits Coins: The Art Institute of Chicago, CC0 (public domain), photographs by the museum. Cloth: *Fragment of a Tunic*, Egypt, Byzantine period, 400s-600s, tabby weave with inwoven tapestry ornament, linen and wool, The Cleveland Museum of Art 1946.413, CC0. One entry per object, with object page, source file, date and dimensions: `assets/credits.json`. Demo data: reign lengths and ages are from the usual dates for each emperor. Aqueduct lengths are Frontinus's, from *De aquaeductu*, converted at a thousand paces to the Roman mile.

# Pick note (sf-chart, 2026-11-03)

**Picked: Roman silver, denarii with quinarii as halves, from the Art Institute of Chicago (CC0), counted out on a
wool tunic fragment from Egypt, 400s-600s (Cleveland Museum of Art 1946.413, CC0).**
187 denarii and quinarii were cut (both pages of AIC's search). After culling the worn ones, two "quinarii" bigger
than many denarii, and every coin whose obverse measures darker than 0.38 lightness or more cast than 0.08 (the
purple-black toners, `tone.py`, sheet `sf-chart-work/sheet-dark.png`), the pool is 144 denarii and 3 quinarii.

## Contact sheets (in `tools/engine/jobs/`)

- `sf-chart-commons1/hunt/sheet.png`: tally sticks, quipu/khipu, strings of cash coins, Salamis tablet, Roman hand abacus (33).
- `sf-chart-commons2/hunt/sheet.png`: Henry III long-cross pennies, cut halfpennies and farthings, Edward I pennies, Athenian owls (62).
- `sf-chart-hunt/sheet-denarii.png`: Art Institute of Chicago Roman coins, all denominations (131).
- `sf-chart-hunt/sheet-cma.png`: Cleveland Museum of Art Greek, Roman, Byzantine and English coins (150 of 556).
- `sf-chart-hunt/pool-obverse.png`, `pool-reverse.png`: the cut pool, both faces, to scale.
- Met Open Access search logs: `sf-chart-hunt/log-*.txt` (few usable coins; no quipu, tallies or wampum with images).

## Shortlist

1. **Roman denarii + quinarii, AIC.** One studio, one light, one flat grey ground (exactly 113 grey, sd 0.2), 3000 px
   masters with each face 500-1150 px across. Every face passed `engine.py inspect`. The diameter is recorded per coin, so
   each one keeps its true size. The quinarius is the real half-denarius (V against X), so halves are real coins too.
2. **English long-cross pennies with real cut halves and quarters** (Portable Antiquities Scheme, Commons, CC BY / BY-SA).
   The craft is lovely: Henry III's long cross was made to guide the shears, so fractions are real cut pieces. But they
   are worn field finds, shot on mixed grounds with scale bars in the frame, and too few are sharp and clean. Second.
3. **Athenian owl tetradrachms** (Cleveland 9, AIC 4, Commons). Mostly case photos, under glass or on black velvet.
   Too few for a pool that never repeats a coin.
4. **Strings of cash coins** (Commons CC0, 5184 px). Real, but grimy clumps. You can't count units in them.
5. Quipu, tally sticks, abacus: museum-case photographs through glass, and none of them reads as a chart at a glance.

## Why this one

A bar chart's job is "how many of a unit", and the denarius was Rome's unit of account: X, ten asses, struck on it.
Every coin is a separate photograph of a separate hand-struck coin, so any value is built from real, interchangeable
units, never a stretched picture. And the half is a real half.

## Second pass: the ground (2026-11-03, after the lead's review)

The coins floated on page colour. Hunted a real surface to lay them on:

- `sf-chart-surface1/hunt/sheet.png`: Rechentisch and counting tables (Strasbourg, Basel), Rechenbrett, Rechentuch,
  Roman marble tables, Matsys's *Moneylender and his Wife*, Reymerswaele's money-changers (32).
- `sf-chart-surface2/hunt/sheet.png`: the Salamis tablet (no photograph on Commons), cartibulum and Pompeii tables,
  Diocletian's mensa (6).
- `sf-chart-hunt/sheet-tex.png`: Cleveland's large CC0 textiles from Roman and Byzantine Egypt (12 of ~180).

Shortlist:
1. **Wool tunic fragment, Egypt, 400s-600s, Cleveland 1946.413 (picked).** Saffron tabby, 64 × 39 cm, a plain field
   156 mm tall between two tapestry bands with a corner band at the left. The full TIFF is 6345 px (9.9 px/mm),
   sharp to the thread. It is Roman-world cloth, Coptic textiles are on Connor's loved list, and the field between
   the bands is a counting area.
2. Strasbourg *Table à calculer des receveurs de l'Œuvre Notre-Dame* (CC BY-SA 4.0): a real counting table with
   bone-inlaid lines and *lib*. But it is 16th-century, its lines are ~15 cm apart, and the wood is plain.
3. Matsys and Reymerswaele: a painted green cloth with painted coins. Photographed coins on painted cloth mix two
   kinds of picture.
4. Undyed tunic sections (Cleveland 1993.177, 1914.800): beautiful, but more loss than cloth.
